title: Where the Weather Sends You
short: Out the window is Souda Bay, about 15 km long and one of the deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, sheltered from the north by the Akrotiri peninsula. Ships have been coming here when the wind says so for centuries, and in 1645, when Chania surrendered, townspeople who chose to leave were ferried across to the Venetian fort on the islet in the bay, which held out until 1715. On the shore lies the Commonwealth war cemetery, where families chose the words on the stones, while warships now sit across the water. Your shuttle sets you down by the Market Hall, about 25 minutes away.
long:
Out over the water, Souda Bay is about 15 km long, usually described as one of the largest and deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, and the long arm of the Akrotiri peninsula to the north keeps most of the sea out of it. This is why Scarlet Lady is here: the wind closed Mykonos to you this morning, and a ship in trouble with the weather has been coming to this bay for as long as there have been ships. Chania itself lies 7 km along the coast.

The small island near the mouth of the bay was fortified by Venice, with the main works usually dated to the 1570s, because whoever held it controlled the way in. It matters most for a day in August 1645, when the Ottomans, having taken Chania after a siege of 56 days, allowed the Venetian garrison and any townspeople who wished to leave to be evacuated, unharmed, to Souda under the surrender terms. For a household that meant a few hours to decide whether to stay in the house the family had lived in, under new masters, or to leave it, and then to choose what would fit in a boat; some of those families had been in Chania since the 1250s, when the Venetians founded the town. Chania fell, but the island did not, and Souda, Gramvousa and Spinalonga stayed Venetian even after Candia surrendered in 1669, Souda holding out until 1715, 70 years after the city behind it. Under the Ottomans the same rock later sheltered Cretan insurgents, so that for ordinary people on this coast an island fortress was part of the landscape of choices, a place to be sent and a place to run to.

A different set of workers uses the same depth of water today, and across the bay you will see grey warships, since Souda Bay hosts Greek naval facilities, a US naval support base and a NATO pier, with a NATO missile firing range up on Akrotiri. A bay that sheltered Venetian galleys now shelters the alliance's navies.

The quieter presence on this shore is Souda Bay War Cemetery, about 1.5 km from the port and beside the water, run by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and holding 1,564 burials. The Battle of Crete lasted from 20 May to 1 June 1941 and was the first invasion in history carried out mainly from the air, with the decisive fighting at Maleme airfield, west of Chania. The graves here are mostly British (862), followed by New Zealand (446) and Australian (197), with a few South African, Canadian and Indian burials, and many are unidentified. Where the name is known there is often a line of personal inscription at the foot of the stone, chosen by families a very long way from here, and anyone who stops to read them is reading the household history of this bay: farm boys from Otago and Queensland and clerks from London, and the people at home who had to decide what a stone should say in a few lines.

Crete's civilians were part of that battle too, and the Maritime Museum later today has a gallery on 1941 that is about villagers as much as soldiers, since the stories of Cretan families fighting the paratroopers with whatever they had are well known on the island.

Greek myth gave Crete a bronze guardian, Talos, who circled the island three times a day and stoned any strange ship that came near. The poem that tells it was written by Apollonius of Rhodes, who links it to the island you toured two days ago, and these days strange ships are allowed in, to the harbour's benefit. The shuttle (or the number 13 bus) takes about 25 minutes and puts you down near the Market Hall, the big cross-shaped building with its doors shut for restoration, which is your next stop.

title: One Roof, Every Trade
short: This cross-shaped hall is Chania's Municipal Market, begun in 1911 and, reportedly, modelled on Marseille's covered market. It stands on the stump of a Venetian bastion called Piatta Forma, so the town's shopping floor replaced a defence, and Prime Minister Venizelos opened it on 4 December 1913, three days after Crete united with Greece. Its four wings hold 76 shops, traditionally butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers and cheese and herb sellers under one roof. It is closed for restoration today (reopening announced for 4 December 2026), so admire it from outside and then walk north-east about 7 minutes to Splantzia.
long:
The doors of the building in front of you are shut, which matters less than it might, because the outside tells most of the story. The Municipal Market is a cross, with four wings and an entrance facing each point of the compass and 76 shops grouped around the arms. Building began in 1911, and several tourism sources say the plan was modelled on the covered market of Marseille, a claim that is repeated more often than it is proven. It is closed for restoration, with its reopening announced for 4 December 2026, so what you see is the shell of a place that is normally loud.

The hall stands on the remains of a Venetian bastion called Piatta Forma, part of the line of walls on the eastern side of the city, and part of those walls was demolished to make room, one piece of the clearing of the old defences that went on in the early 20th century as the town outgrew them. For a household historian the exchange is a good one: the wall that kept 16th-century families in was removed so that 20th-century families could shop. Behind the walls the town had been cramped, while outside them there was space for a building with air, light and running water, which in those years counted as civic virtue, and a single hall with standard stalls replaced the scattered street markets in the name of public hygiene and pride in a brand-new Greek town.

The timing explains much of the ambition. The Greek flag went up at Firkas on 1 December 1913, the formal moment of Crete's union with Greece, and three days later Eleftherios Venizelos, who was born just outside Chania and was by then Prime Minister of Greece, came home to open the market, so that a covered market became a statement that this was now a modern city in a Greek state. A household in 1913 had changed flags without moving house: the people who bought bread, cheese and fish here had been Ottoman subjects, then residents of an autonomous Cretan State under four Great Powers for 15 years, and were now Greek citizens.

The wings were traditionally divided by trade, with butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers, and sellers of cheese and herbs, although which wing held which trade is not recorded in anything easy to check, so the layout is best taken loosely. What matters is how a household used a place like this, with someone walking the arms of the cross with a basket, knowing which stall had good mizithra (the soft fresh cheese that goes on dakos, the barley rusk with tomato) and which seller would weigh fairly. Crete's food has always depended on that kind of knowledge, and on wild greens (horta) from the hills, olive oil from the family trees, snails after rain and cheese pies called kalitsounia, so that when you eat later you will find how much of it never comes from a shop at all.

This spot is also a good place to stand back and set out the layers of the town, because everything else today stacks on them. Under the hill ahead of you, Kastelli, lies Minoan Kydonia, followed by Greek and Roman Kydonia (the Romans took Crete in 69 BC) and by Byzantine rule, which was interrupted by the Arab Emirate of Crete from 824 to 961, until Nikephoros Phokas took the island back. In 1252 Venetian colonists founded La Canea on the old site, and Venice held it until 1645, when the Ottomans took the city after 56 days. Ottoman rule lasted until 1898, with a short Egyptian interlude from the 1830s to 1840, and was followed by the Cretan State, with Chania as its capital, from 1898 to 1913, and then by Greece. Each change altered things differently for different groups, in who paid which tax, which building was a church and which a mosque, who could own land near the harbour and who had to leave, and the rest of the morning follows those changes through ordinary lives.

If the wind is strong you will feel it funnel along the street here. Walk north-east with the sea on your left and the old town on your right for about 7 minutes to Splantzia, a square with a plane tree and, on its church, both a minaret and a bell tower. Coffee is waiting under the tree, and with it the story of what happened to a quarter of the city in 1923.

title: A Minaret and a Bell
short: You are in Plateia 1821, Splantzia, the old Muslim quarter, facing the church of Agios Nikolaos, built around 1320 by Dominican friars, turned into the Sultan's mosque after 1645 and Orthodox again since 1918. It wears a minaret (about 36 m) and a bell tower added in the 1950s, reportedly a combination found nowhere else in Greece. Neighbours here spoke the same Greek and prayed in different buildings until the 1923 population exchange sent the Muslim families away, and the story that the big plane tree was used for hangings is legend. Have coffee at Platanos, then walk 4 minutes west, uphill, to Kastelli.
long:
You are in Plateia 1821, in the district called Splantzia, from the Venetian word for piazza. The big plane tree stands in front of you with coffee tables beneath it, and across the square rises a church with a tall round minaret beside a bell tower, a pairing that holds most of the neighbourhood's history in a single building.

The church is Agios Nikolaos, built around 1320 by Dominican friars as a Roman Catholic monastery church, in the Venetian period, when the Dominicans of Candia ran a brotherhood here. After the Ottomans took the city in 1645 it was one of three churches converted into mosques right away, and it became the Hünkar Camii, the Sultan's Mosque, named for Sultan Ibrahim, who had launched the war. The cylindrical minaret is about 36 m tall and would have topped 40 with its lost conical cap. In 1918 the building was reconsecrated as an Orthodox church dedicated to St Nicholas, and the bell tower was added in the 1950s, which is why it is often called the only building in Greece with both a minaret and a bell tower, although that is widely repeated rather than proven. It is a working church, usually open in the daytime outside services and free to enter, and worth a quiet look if you are dressed for it.

Imagine the square on an ordinary morning in, say, the 18th century. Splantzia was the heart of the Muslim quarter, Topanas to the west was the Christian quarter, and the Jewish quarter, Evraiki, lay a few streets away, though the labels flatter the neatness of it. Many of the Muslims here were Cretans whose families had converted over the generations after 1645, and they spoke Greek, ate the same food, followed the same seasons and heard the same music as their Christian neighbours, so that the differences lay in which building they entered on Friday or on Sunday, what taxes they paid and what the law allowed them. A tradition says that the small church of Agioi Anargyroi, just off the square, was the only place Orthodox Christians were allowed to worship in the city, but it is a tradition and not a checked fact. What the pattern suggests is how life under a conquering faith was organised day to day, through negotiation, with households finding workable arrangements with the neighbours on both sides of the wall.

The plane tree has a tale of its own that comes with a warning. Local tradition says that Ottoman authorities hanged Orthodox clergy and rebels from it, and that the bishop of Kissamos, Melchisedek Despotakis, was hanged here in 1821, but the story has been repeated because it feels right, and the record does not confirm it, so it is best treated as legend. What is solid is that 1821, the year the Greek revolution began, gave the square its name, and that Crete's part in that revolution brought reprisals and rebellion over and over, through the long chain of revolts in the 19th century.

The year that deserves a quiet minute is 1923, when the Treaty of Lausanne had Greece and Turkey exchange populations by religion. Most Cretan Muslims left, many of them from families who had lived here for generations and had never lived anywhere else, speaking Greek to the last, and their houses were taken over by Orthodox refugees from Asia Minor, who were leaving their own homes and had also lost everything. Neither group had much choice, and both were households trying to start again with a few bags, so that the minaret now stands for a community that was here for centuries and then gone.

Platanos, on the square, is good for coffee or a raki under the tree, facing the church and minaret. Raki is often brought free after a meal in Crete, so the habit of hospitality has outlasted every change of flag, and if the weather is turning you can shelter under the tree's canopy for a minute or step into the church.

When you are ready, head about 4 minutes west, uphill, to Kastelli hill, where something much older lies under all of this: a Bronze Age kitchen behind a fence.

title: The Kitchen Under the Hill
short: You are on Kastelli hill, over Minoan Kydonia, and through the fence at Agia Aikaterini square lies a house from about 1450 BC, destroyed by fire. In its kitchen archaeologists found a clay hearth with a loom beside it and a jar of about 3 kg of burnt lentils and vetch, and the same fire baked clay tablets hard, leaving about 99 Linear A accounts and the sealings that locked jars and doors. A later Linear B tablet records honey for Zeus and Dionysos, in effect a receipt for gods, and the quince takes its name from the town. Walk down about 4 minutes to the Neoria on the east harbour.
long:
You are standing on top of a Bronze Age town. Kastelli hill, the low rise behind the harbour, has been lived on almost without a break for about 5,000 years, the one gap being roughly 1150 to 735 BC. From Agia Aikaterini square, on Kanevaro Street, you can look through the fence at a patch of excavation about 600 m² in area, with around 2 m of layers stacked up beneath a protective roof built in 2005 to 2008. Digs began in 1964, and from 1970 the Greek-Swedish excavation took over.

The house you are looking at is called Building 1. It covered 225 m², had two storeys and 14 rooms on the ground floor, and was surrounded by streets and small squares. The detail worth walking a long way for comes from a kitchen, where archaeologists found a clay hearth with a loom beside it, and in a jar about 3 kg of burnt legumes, vetch and lentils or peas, carbonised where they sat, so that someone had evidently been cooking and weaving in the same room. Around 1450 BC a fire swept through, part of a Crete-wide wave of destruction, and the meal was never eaten.

The same fire preserved something else. Clay tablets, which would normally be dried in the sun and then crumble, were baked hard, so that about 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, found in 1973, survive from here, the second-largest archive of this script after Hagia Triada. Most are records of farm produce and livestock, and because Linear A has never been deciphered we can read the numbers and some commodity signs, and so the accounts, but not the words, which means we can count the sheep without being able to say their names. Alongside the tablets were clay sealings, lumps pressed with a seal and stuck over the string on a jar, box or door so that anyone could tell whether it had been opened. One clay bar carries twelve impressions from ten different seals, a piece of bureaucracy in clay in which someone checked who had opened the storeroom.

The most famous find is the Master Impression, a sealing from the second half of the 15th century BC, which shows a long-haired male figure in a kilt, holding a staff or spear, standing over a multi-storey walled town on a rocky shore, with windows and horns of consecration on the buildings. The gold ring that made it has never been found, and scholars argue whether the figure is a ruler or a god and whether the town is Kydonia, none of which can be proved. The walls sit awkwardly with the old idea of a peaceful Minoan Crete, itself a contested notion.

About two centuries later, in 1989 and 1990, archaeologists found five Linear B tablets here, in the Greek of Mycenaean Crete and dated to the 13th century BC. One, called KH Gq 5, records honey, and is read roughly as: to the sanctuary of Zeus; to Zeus, honey, 1 amphora; to Dionysos, honey, 2 amphorae. It sets two later Greek gods side by side, with Dionysos getting double, and shows religion as lived practice and as household economy, with offerings budgeted on the same kind of clay as sheep and wool (that it shows Dionysos already as Zeus's son is a guess, not a finding).

The name of the town is securely written at Knossos, where scribes wrote ku-do-ni-ja in their records, while no tablet found here has yet been shown to carry it, so the safe claim is that Knossos knew this town. Inscribed jars from west Crete turned up at Thebes, traced by clay analysis, and the Knossos tablets list named women as textile workers on rations, so that women clearly worked and took part in ritual, although whether they ruled is unknown and the Minoan matriarchy of popular books is a modern idea, not a finding.

The town gave the world a fruit, since the Greeks called the quince the Kydonian apple and the botanical name Cydonia comes from it (a few linguists suspect an older word was bent to fit the town). Homer mentions the Kydonians, and the founder, King Kydon, is a myth with several versions, while the Minotaur belongs to Knossos.

Above all this the Byzantines built a wall in the 10th century and the Venetians made the hill their Castello, where nobles and officials lived, while Greek artisans and fishermen lived outside until the new walls of 1536 to 1568 enclosed them. From here it is about 4 minutes down to the east harbour and the long stone sheds of the Neoria.

title: Sheds for the Winter Fleet
short: The long arched sheds along the south side are the Venetian Neoria, shipyards built from 1526 to 1599, with 17 vaults here and five more (the Moro yards) on the east side, so about 22 in all, though some sources say 23. Each hall is about 50 m long with an open sea end, so that galleys could be hauled in to be built, mended and kept dry for winter, and in 1645 the Ottomans found 12 galleys inside. In a Moro yard sits Minoa, a lashed, nail-free replica of a Bronze Age ship rowed to Piraeus in 2004. The lighthouse is about 10 minutes out along the breakwater.
long:
The row of long, arched stone sheds on the south side of the harbour is the Neoria, the Venetian shipyards, and it is one of the few places on this walk where a whole working industry still stands in front of you. The first two were finished in 1526, by 1593 there were 16, and the 17th completed the south range in 1599. A few years later five more, the Moro yards, were added on the east side of the harbour, where you are heading, which makes about 22 in all, though some sources say 23 and none can be taken as certain. A row of seven vaulted halls survives together, with one more farther west, the Grand Arsenal, which now houses the Centre of Mediterranean Architecture.

The scale is what impresses. Each hall was about 50 m long, 9 m wide and 10 m high, with arched openings in the side walls linking the halls and the seaward end left open, so that galleys could be hauled straight in on slipways and then built, repaired and kept through the winter, out of the storm season and safe from corsairs.

The sources are thin on who worked here, so this is a reasonable inference and not a record, but shipbuilding on this scale meant carpenters, caulkers, rope-makers and oarsmen, and a ship under repair needed people who could cut timber, drive and seal planks, spin and tar rope, and make sails. The yards were probably the town's biggest employer, and many families would have lived near them because of that.

When the city fell in 1645 the Ottomans walked into the arsenal and found 12 Venetian galleys sitting in the sheds, and the buildings outlived their owners. Later uses reportedly included Ottoman and Egyptian military stores and then 20th-century warehouses and workshops, though the details are thin, and a war factory is now in part an architecture centre, having kept finding new work.

The Moro shipyard at the east end holds the exhibit most worth seeing. Minoa is an experimental replica of a Minoan ship of the 16th to 15th centuries BC, about 17 m long and about 4 m wide, built from 2001 to 2004 of split cypress planks lashed and sewn together, not nailed, with oars and a single square sail. The design drew on ship images such as the Akrotiri flotilla fresco on Santorini and on seals, and in 2004 the ship was rowed and sailed some 210 nautical miles from Chania to Piraeus for the Athens Olympics, meeting the Olympic flame at the end. The annex is part of the Maritime Museum, with entry of about 3 euros and opening until 31 October, while the Maritime Museum itself has its own hours and a separate ticket, and you will pass it later.

Beside a hull like that it is easy to think of the household around it, since someone had to cut the cypress, split the planks, make the rope that lashes them, weave the sail and feed the crew who would row. An old Greek source adds a line that is best held lightly: Thucydides says Minos was the first to build a navy and that he cleared the sea of pirates so that his revenues could come in. Whether there was ever a Minoan naval empire is argued over, and scholars today tend to prefer a picture of trade and cultural influence, but the Minoan ships were real, jars exported from this town turned up on the mainland, and the sea is the island's long constant.

If the weather is dry enough, go out along the breakwater to the lighthouse, about 10 minutes away, bearing in mind that the stones can be wet and slippery and spray may come over, in which case you can skip it and take the view from the quay. The lighthouse looks a little like a minaret, for a reason that comes next.

title: The Tower at the Harbour Mouth
short: You are at the end of the breakwater beside a tower with an octagonal base, a 16-sided middle and a round top, built to bring boats, cargo and fishing families home past these rocks. Venice built the first light here in the late 16th century, and the tower you see is a 19th-century rebuild (local accounts say about 1839, under Egypt; other sources say 1864), whose shape is why people call it minaret-like. Looking back, you see the working waterfront as it appears from the sea. If the spray is coming over, turn around here; otherwise it is about 15 minutes back along the breakwater and round the harbour to the domed mosque.
long:
You are at the end of the breakwater beside the lighthouse, whose tower has an octagonal base, a 16-sided middle section and a round top, all built of stone with a stair inside. The path out here is uneven, so if the sea is coming over the wall and the stones are wet, this is the place to turn back; if it is safe, you are about 600 metres from where the breakwater begins, standing in a spot that exists for one reason, which is to get ordinary working boats home.

A harbour like this is less about the grand ships than about the caique that left before dawn and has to find the gap between the rocks in a north wind, the cargo boat carrying oil or wine or cloth, the porter waiting on the quay, the customs man and the wife who watches the horizon from a kitchen window, and a light is a promise made to all of them. Venice built the first one at the end of this breakwater in the late 16th century, usually dated 1595 to 1601. After the Ottoman conquest in 1645 it fell into neglect, as often happens when the flag changes and the soldiers and tax collectors arrive well before the maintenance budget does.

The tower you see is a 19th-century rebuild, and sources disagree on when. The most common local account puts it around 1839, during the ten years (1830 to 1840) when Crete was ruled from Egypt by Mehmet Ali, which is why it is sometimes called the Egyptian lighthouse, while other sources say 1864, and it is fair to carry both dates and not choose. Either way it went up under a regime that was neither Venetian nor yet Greek, and its octagon and stair gave it the look of a minaret, a practical building quietly outliving the people who commissioned it.

The Egyptian decade was short and odd, with some tax reforms, some public works, a rebuilt lighthouse and a good deal of unrest, and for most households the question was the one it always is when rulers change: who collects the tax, and how much is left on the table. A fixed white light was installed in May 1915, making this an official lighthouse of the Greek service two years after Crete joined Greece. Today it flashes red every 2.5 seconds and is visible about 7 nautical miles out; it was damaged in the Second World War and restored in 2005 to 2006. Nothing documented names the keepers or harbour workers of any period, though a light like this needs someone to climb that stair, which is worth picturing as you stand here.

There is an older kind of care on this coast, too. West of Chania, on the tip of the Rodopou peninsula, lies the sanctuary of Diktynna, whose name comes from the Greek word for a net. Legend says she threw herself from a cliff to escape King Minos and was caught in fishermen's nets, becoming their goddess; that is a myth, and the sanctuary's oldest finds date only from the late 7th or 6th century BC, so it is not shown to be Minoan, but it is a lovely detail that fishing families prayed to a goddess of the net because the net was how they ate.

Turning back, you get the best view of the whole waterfront, with the quay, the mosque dome, the old shipyards and the houses stacked behind, which is the working street of the town seen from the sea. For generations the walk out here has been a family ritual, an evening stroll along the sea wall, and you can see who is taking it today in whatever weather you have been given.

When you are ready, head back along the breakwater and then round the harbour; it is about 15 minutes along the quay to the low domed mosque, the next stop.

title: The Neighbours' Mosque by the Sea
short: The squat building with the big dome and a row of small domes over its porch is the Kioutsouk Hasan mosque, also called Yiali Tzamisi, the Seaside Mosque. It went up from 1645, right after the Ottoman conquest, and is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete, named for Küçük (Little) Hasan Pasha, the first Ottoman commander. The minaret is gone, but you can imagine a neighbourhood fixture on the quay, with prayer, coffee and trade within a few steps of each other. After 1923 it served as a warehouse, a museum and a tourist office, and it now opens only for exhibitions, so look for a sign. Walk west along the harbour, about 5 minutes, to Firkas.
long:
You are standing in front of the Kioutsouk Hasan mosque, called Yiali Tzamisi, the Seaside Mosque, by the Greeks. It has a large hemispherical dome on four great arches and a row of smaller domes over the porch (sources count six or seven, so you may want to count them yourself). A minaret once stood here and was demolished in the 20th century, in the 1920s or by 1939 depending on the source. The building opens only for temporary exhibitions, so check the door, though it is worth seeing from outside in any case.

It was built from 1645, straight after the Ottoman conquest, and is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete, with some sources giving 1645 and others 1645 to 1649. The name is Küçük, "Little", Hasan Pasha, given as the first Ottoman commander of the city, and it is also known as the Mosque of the Janissaries. Tradition names an Armenian architect, which is better taken as a story than a record.

The town came to this point by way of a war that began in 1644, when the Knights of Malta captured an Ottoman ship, reportedly carrying a member of the Sultan's harem, and put in on Crete, and Sultan Ibrahim blamed Venice. The Ottoman fleet left Istanbul on 30 April 1645 and reached Chania in late June, and the siege lasted 56 days (some sources say 54 or 57), ending on 22 August. Roughly 50,000 men and 416 ships came against about 12,000 defenders, mostly local militia rather than professional soldiers, and a commander named Blasio Zulian, who held the little fort on the islet offshore with 30 men, chose to blow it up with himself and them inside rather than surrender. The Venetian garrison and townspeople who wished to leave were evacuated unharmed to Souda, and the war moved on to Candia (Heraklion), where it lasted about 21 years.

What a conquest means on an ordinary street is easier to see from here. Straight after the surrender three churches in Chania became mosques, and Venetian families who could leave did so, while an Ottoman garrison of about 8,000 stayed, and a garrison is not just soldiers but bakers, boatmen, coffee sellers, tailors, women running households and children underfoot. A mosque built on the quay, where the Venetian galleys had once tied up, did several jobs at once: it was a place to pray five times a day, but also a landmark, a meeting point and a sign of who now ran the harbour. What survives is the building and its dates rather than any record of daily life around it, but it is reasonable to picture the quay as a working street, with fishermen, porters, coffee houses and customs men within earshot of the call to prayer.

The population that used it was more mixed than the word "Ottoman" suggests. Over the following generations many Cretans converted, so that Muslims in Chania were often Greek-speaking Cretans living next to Orthodox Christians and a Jewish community in a quarter of its own; Splantzia, where you stood earlier, was the Muslim quarter, and Topanas, where you are going, was the Christian one. They shared a language, a cuisine and a good deal of music while praying in different buildings, until 1923, when the population exchange following the Treaty of Lausanne sent most Cretan Muslims away and the mosques lost their congregations almost overnight.

The building's later history follows the city's changing priorities: it became a warehouse, then the Archaeological Museum, then an office of the Greek Tourism Organisation, and it now belongs to the Port Fund and is used for exhibitions. It has survived, as buildings that outlast their original purpose usually do, because it has been useful to every regime since.

With your back to the sea you can take in the dome, the harbour and the people walking past, and then continue west along the waterfront; it is about 5 minutes to Firkas, the fortress at the harbour's western mouth.

title: Barracks, Prison and a Flag
short: Before you is Firkas, the Venetian bastion at the western mouth of the harbour, whose name comes from the Turkish firka, barracks; under the Ottomans it was a barracks and a prison, with hundreds of men eating, sleeping and waiting inside these walls. On 1 December 1913 the Greek flag went up here for Crete's union with Greece. Today it holds the Maritime Museum of Crete (09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros), with Bronze Age ship models, Venetian galleys and a Battle of Crete gallery, and the caique tools and nets on display show a fishing family's living. From here walk about 5 minutes south into Topanas and the old Jewish quarter.
long:
You are at Firkas, the fortress at the west end of the harbour, built in 1620 beside the San Salvatore bastion at the north-west corner of the walls to guard the harbour mouth. Its name gives away what came next, since firka is Turkish for barracks, and under the Ottomans this was a barracks and a prison. The museum inside, the Maritime Museum of Crete (open 09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros), was founded in 1973.

After 1645 about 8,000 soldiers were left to hold Chania, and they had to be housed, fed and kept in order somewhere; a garrison eats grain, meat and oil every day, wears out boots, and needs water, fuel and bread. The same buildings held prisoners, and a prison, then as now, was a household of its own, in which feeding the inmates fell in many places in the period partly to their families, who came to the gate with bread. That cannot be documented for Firkas, so it is best taken as the general pattern rather than a local fact, but every flag that flew here certainly relied on ordinary people to keep it supplied.

The 19th century brought a run of Cretan revolts, in 1866 to 1869 (remembered most for Arkadi monastery, near Rethymno, where defenders blew up their powder store rather than surrender), then in 1878, 1889 and 1895 to 1897. In each, villages emptied, women and children took shelter in monasteries, and families had a man up in the mountains. The 1878 Pact of Halepa gave Crete limited home rule, a rare case of a revolt leading to paperwork that actually changed how people were governed.

In 1898 the Great Powers (Britain, France, Russia and Italy) set up the autonomous Cretan State with Chania as its capital, which is why the town had consuls and a prince: Prince George of Greece was High Commissioner, living in Halepa, the district east of the old town. Eleftherios Venizelos, born in 1864 at Mournies just outside Chania, was a local lawyer-politician who led the Theriso revolt in 1905 against Prince George's rule and in 1910 went to Athens and became Prime Minister of Greece. A rebel turned prime minister makes a good story, but for a household his career matters more as a measure of what it took to change who made the rules.

The decisive date is 1 December 1913. Under the Treaty of London of 30 May 1913 the Ottoman Empire gave up its rights to Crete, and on this fortress the Greek flag was raised, with King Constantine and Venizelos attending. Three days later, on 4 December, Venizelos opened the new Municipal Market, which you saw this morning, so that the flag came first and the shops after, as if a fresh political identity needed a modern place to buy cheese and fish.

The changes fell differently on different people: for Orthodox families the end of Ottoman rule meant an end to second-class status, for Cretan Muslims it began the last years before the 1923 exchange, and the capital stayed in Chania until 1971, when it moved to Heraklion.

If the weather is bad, the museum is the place to go in, and the Bronze Age room has models of Minoan ships and finds from underwater archaeology, alongside Venetian galleys and a section on traditional boatbuilding, with caiques, nets and tools that show how a fishing or boatbuilding family made a living under all the flags. The Battle of Crete gallery is about civilians as much as soldiers, since Cretan villagers fought paratroopers with whatever they had. Entry is 4 euros, and it closes at 17:00.

When you come out, walk about 5 minutes south, away from the water, into Topanas, the Venetian nobles' quarter and later the Christian quarter, just beyond which is the old Jewish quarter, Evraiki.

title: The Courtyard of Evraiki
short: You are in the lanes of Evraiki, the old Jewish quarter, at the Etz Hayyim synagogue on Parodos Kondylaki, which began as a Venetian church and became a synagogue in the 17th century, and where a community prayed, studied and lived for centuries beside Christian and Muslim neighbours. In May 1944 the Germans arrested Chania's Jews, about 250 to 275 people, and on 9 June the ship carrying them, the Tanais, was sunk by a British submarine that did not know who was aboard. The building was restored and reopened in 1999, and today it is open until 15:00 (4 euros, with a short tour); please photograph the building only. Lunch is two minutes away at Tamam.
long:
You are at Etz Hayyim, on Parodos Kondylaki, in the streets of Evraiki, the Jewish quarter of Chania, a place that asks for quiet and an unhurried visit. It is open today until 15:00; entry is 4 euros, which includes a short tour with the staff, and they ask that you photograph the building only, with no selfies. The tour is worth taking if you can.

The building began as a church in the Venetian period and became a synagogue in the 17th century, after the Ottoman conquest, and a Jewish community lived in this quarter under both the Venetians and the Ottomans. It was a Romaniote community, one of the Greek-speaking Jewish traditions, whose roots on Crete are described as going back to antiquity, though what can be said with confidence here is limited to what is documented and what the place itself shows. A synagogue in a small quarter is usually more than a room for prayer, being also where the community gathers for the big moments of life, and the courtyard, the garden and the mikveh, the ritual bath, show that this was a house of daily life as well as worship.

What the visit makes plain is how normal it was. For centuries Jewish families in Chania lived in a mixed town, a few streets from Splantzia's Muslim quarter and Topanas's Christian one, trading in the same markets, speaking the same Greek and keeping their own calendar of festivals.

On 29 May 1944, during the German occupation, soldiers rounded up the Jews of Chania, about 250 to 275 people (another account gives 276 arrested on 20 May, so sources differ on the exact date and number). They were taken by truck to Heraklion and put on board a ship, the Tanais, together with Greek hostages, resistance prisoners and Italian prisoners of war, and on 9 June 1944 the British submarine HMS Vivid fired four torpedoes at about 2,400 yards. Two hit, and the ship sank in about 12 seconds, north-west of the islet of Dia, with the crew of the Vivid unaware of who was aboard. Estimates of the dead run from 425 to 1,000, about 265 of them Cretan Jews, and the sinking ended Crete's Jewish community. The Tanais had been sunk once before, by the Luftwaffe in Souda Bay in May 1941, and then raised and repaired. A memorial to the victims stands in Chania, and the town marks the anniversary each June.

After the war the synagogue was a ruin, and it was restored in the late 1990s, with Nikos Stavroulakis leading the work, and reopened in 1999. Arsonists attacked it on 5 and 16 January 2010, and the second fire destroyed about 2,500 rare books and manuscripts, after which it was repaired again. Today the congregation is mostly non-Jewish, follows Sephardic customs and has written its own Haggadah, so that in effect people who live here look after a house of prayer whose own community is gone. In 2006 Queen Sofia of Spain and the former King Constantine II visited unannounced.

If the staff show you the memorial plaque, it lists the deported families by name, a reminder of the households behind a day otherwise given to cannon and flag.

Take a moment in the courtyard, then go to lunch at Tamam, on Zambeliou, about two minutes away in a former hammam (Ottoman bath), where the Cretan-Ottoman cooking indoors suits this weather. After lunch, a taxi east to the Archaeological Museum at Chalepa is kinder in the rain than the 25-minute walk.

title: The Ledger and the Hearth
short: This is the Archaeological Museum of Chania at Skra 15, Chalepa, open 08:00 to 20:00 (15 euros with audio guide), which opened in 2022 and whose best pieces are small: the Master Impression, a tiny clay sealing from Kastelli, and the tablets, Linear A accounts and a Linear B tablet recording honey for Zeus and Dionysos, which are household and temple bookkeeping. There is also a painted clay coffin from Armeni (a cemetery near Rethymno) and everyday Minoan pottery, and together they show people keeping stores, counting them and feeding their gods, the thread running through the whole day. Take a taxi back to Souda in time for the ship by 18:00.
long:
You are at the Archaeological Museum of Chania, at Skra 15 in Chalepa, which opened in April 2022 to replace the old museum in the Venetian church of San Francesco in the old town. It is open 08:00 to 20:00, with entry at 15 euros including an audio guide, and if you are wet and tired you have chosen well. The floor plan at the entrance is worth checking, since the rooms may be arranged differently from what is described here.

The best pieces are small, and almost all of them concern the management of a household, which links them to the Minoan town on Kastelli hill that you stood above this morning. The sealings are lumps of clay stamped with a seal and pressed onto jar stoppers, boxes and doors, so that anyone opening a storeroom had to break the seal; the excavation turned up a clay bar bearing twelve seal impressions from ten different seals. Then comes the Master Impression itself, a tiny sealing a few centimetres across showing a tall figure over a walled, multi-storey town by the sea. The gold ring that made it has never been found, and whether the figure is a ruler, a god or a ruler shown as divine is argued over, so it is best left unsettled.

The tablets come next. Kydonia produced something like 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, the second-largest archive of that script after Hagia Triada, mostly records of farm produce and livestock, and they survive because the fire around 1450 BC baked them hard. No one can read Linear A as language, but the numbers and some commodity signs can be read, so the accounts can be followed without the words. If it is on display, a Linear B tablet records honey, roughly "to Zeus, honey", one amphora, and "to Dionysos, honey", two; it is about 800 years older than classical Greek drama, and it shows religion as a line in the household budget, written on the same kind of clay as sheep and wool. The idea that it proves Dionysos was already Zeus's son is an inference, and a debated one.

The kitchen seen through the fence earlier, with a clay hearth and a loom beside it and a jar holding about 3 kilograms of burnt lentils and vetch, belongs with these records, since the hearth, the cloth and the clerk upstairs counting make a household together. In Linear B records from Knossos, textile workers appear by name on ration lists, women and children among them, so that women's work was real and measured, although whether women held political power is unknown and the "matriarchy" idea is a modern projection, not evidence.

The larnakes, painted clay coffins, include one decorated with a hunting scene; it comes from a cemetery at Armeni, near Rethymno, not Chania, and dates like the others to 1400 to 1200 BC. The pottery includes the "Kydonia workshop" wares of the 13th century BC and large inscribed stirrup jars, oil or wine jars painted in Linear B, which clay analysis traces to west Crete and some of which turned up at Thebes; a jar like that is the Bronze Age equivalent of a shipping label. Beyond them are the later cities, Greek and Roman Kydonia, laid down in layers.

Chalepa itself adds a last point. In the Cretan State, from 1898 to 1913, this eastern district was where consuls and the prince's court lived, and the Venizelos house is here, so that while the old town's harbour had galleys and then a garrison, Chalepa had a tidier world of diplomats and lawyers' households, each era arranging its people differently.

The day closes where it began, with the people under the hill who counted their oil, wove their wool and gave honey to the gods, while the Venetians built their shipyards, the Ottomans their mosques and the town its market and its synagogue, and underneath them the same questions about storage, work and neighbours kept coming round.

To go home, a taxi from here to Souda is the easiest way to be back on the ship before 18:00, and in the rain it is wise to allow plenty of time and a margin.
